::: {.why}
Ruin is not the 99th percentile of a return distribution, it is an absorbing state, and the difference matters because leverage and margin can put you there before the statistics do.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Compute the probability of hitting a ruin threshold before a target, and connect it to the gambler's ruin result you drilled in week 16.
- Say what a margin call does to the calculation, and why it makes the barrier higher than the one you chose.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Do the calculation both ways and reconcile them: the diffusion approximation for hitting a lower barrier before an upper one, and the direct simulation of your strategy's returns. Report both for your chosen leverage.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Add the mechanical barrier from day 13: at your leverage and your broker's maintenance margin, compute the loss that triggers a call. That level is a hard barrier well above zero, and the ruin probability that matters is the probability of touching it, not of losing everything.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Add `risk_of_ruin()` to qlib/portfolio.py taking leverage, maintenance margin and return parameters, with the barrier computed rather than passed in.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
The book's sizing now respects a hard barrier derived from maintenance margin rather than a soft statistical threshold, and qlib/portfolio.py computes the ruin probability from leverage and margin directly.
:::
